item.title: Guide to Compliance and Cybersecurity in Healthcare Software Development
item.description:
In healthcare software, compliance and cybersecurity are not merely administrative procedures, they are integral features of the product itself. According to IBM’s “2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report,” the healthcare industry has recorded the highest average cost of a data breach across all industries for 13 consecutive years, with the cost per incident reaching $6.64 million. Meanwhile, AI-enabled attacks have increased the cost per data breach across all industries by approximately $1 million.

The 2024 ransomware attack on Change Healthcare is recorded as the largest data breach in the history of the healthcare industry, with data from approximately 192.7 million people compromised. This attack originated from a single portal that lacked multi-factor authentication.

This guide explains the applicable regulations, a step-by-step process for building secure and compliant software, and the best development companies to assist with this effort.

The Regulatory Landscape

Which rules apply depends on what data your product touches, who your customers are and where your users live. Most healthcare products answer to more than one framework at once.

  1. HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (US). Apply to covered entities and their business associates, including vendors that store or process PHI. Expect risk analysis, access controls, audit logs, encryption and a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA). The Security Rule overhaul proposed in January 2025 is now targeted for July 2027.
  2. HIPAA Breach Notification Rule and HITECH Act (US). Require notifying patients and HHS of a breach, generally within 60 days of discovery.
  3. FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (US). Covers health apps and wearables outside HIPAA, including unauthorized data sharing. The 2024 amendments remain in force; in September 2026 the FTC withdrew its older 2021 policy statement as redundant.
  4. FDA cybersecurity requirements (US). Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and connected devices need threat modeling, a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and a vulnerability-management plan.
  5. State health privacy laws (US). Laws such as Washington’s My Health My Data Act require consent for consumer health data and limit its sale.
  6. GDPR and UK GDPR. Health data is a special category, requiring an explicit legal basis, DPIAs and 72-hour breach notice to regulators.
  7. EU Health Data Space and AI Act. EHDS security and interoperability rules for EHR systems apply from March 2029. A provisional May 2026 deal would delay AI Act obligations for AI in medical devices to August 2028.

The pending HIPAA Security Rule update shows where enforcement is heading: mandatory MFA, encryption, asset inventories and annual audits. Building those in now is cheaper than retrofitting later.

Step-by-step guide to building compliant, secure healthcare software

Step 1: Map your data and regulatory scope

Let’s start by creating a data inventory. Determine what types of health data you are collecting, where that data flows, who has access to it, and which third parties receive it. Next, classify each data type according to the framework described above.

This will determine whether a BAA, a DPIA, or FDA approval is required or perhaps all of them. Be sure to document the results of this classification, as they will be requested by auditors and the hospital’s security team.

Step 2: Run a risk analysis and design for privacy

A documented risk assessment is the foundation for HIPAA compliance, and the OCR cites the lack of such an assessment more often than any other violation of the security rules. Combine this with threat modeling for each function that handles PHI. Collect only the data that each function needs, use anonymized data for analysis and testing, and never copy PHI from the production environment to development environments.

Step 3: Build a secure architecture with encryption

Segment networks so that PHI storage locations are kept separate from services accessible to the general public, implement “zero-trust” principles, and select cloud services covered by the provider’s BAA. Plan for high availability, as downtime in clinical software poses a risk to patient safety.

Encrypt PHI at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2 or higher), and store keys in a managed key service with scheduled rotation. IBM’s 2026 report showed that 53% of organizations that had suffered a data breach had not encrypted sensitive data.

Step 4: Lock down access and log every action

Require multi-factor authentication for all users with access to PHI, and implement role-based access according to the “least privilege” principle. Implement session time limits and a documented “break-glass” procedure for clinical access in emergencies. Maintain audit logs showing who has viewed, modified, or exported which medical records, and issue alerts for unusual patterns, such as bulk exports.

Step 5: Secure the development lifecycle and integrations

Base coding standards on OWASP guidance, run static and dynamic security testing in the CI/CD pipeline and scan open-source dependencies. Commission independent penetration tests before launch and at least yearly. For integrations, use HL7 FHIR with OAuth 2.0 and SMART on FHIR scopes, sign BAAs with every vendor that handles PHI, and audit tracking pixels and analytics SDKs.

Step 6: Prepare for incidents and keep compliance continuous

Write and rehearse an incident response plan that covers ransomware and notification deadlines, and keep tested, immutable backups. Notification clocks start at discovery, so decide in advance who declares an incident and who contacts regulators. After launch, treat compliance as ongoing work: annual risk reviews, staff training, vulnerability management and third-party audits such as SOC 2 Type II or HITRUST.

The common thread across all six steps is timing. Teams that treat these controls as everyday engineering work, rather than a checklist before launch, avoid the costly rework that sinks many healthcare projects. As one healthcare IT expert explains:

“The most expensive compliance mistake we see is treating HIPAA or GDPR as a checklist to complete right before launch. By then, the architecture is set, PHI has leaked into logs and test databases, and every fix means rework. Our teams start each healthcare project with a data-flow map and a risk analysis, and we treat encryption, MFA and audit logging as acceptance criteria for every user story. Companies that design security in from day one spend less and ship faster than those that bolt it on later,” Roman Provotorov, Healthcare IT Expert and Consultant at IT Craft Firm.

Best Custom Software Development Firms For Healthcare Compliance And Security

The five firms below (ScienceSoft, IT Craft, Taction Software, HTD Health and Keyhole Software) combine healthcare domain experience with documented security practices, relevant certifications and a track record of delivered healthcare projects. Here is a comparison of them:

1. ScienceSoft

Founded in 1989, ScienceSoft has worked in healthcare IT since 2005 and reports more than 150 completed healthcare projects. It holds ISO 13485, ISO 9001, ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 certifications, and in-house regulatory consultants support HIPAA, GDPR, FDA and MDR work. It signs BAAs from the start of an engagement.

Best for: SaMD and medical-device software that must go through FDA clearance or CE marking.

Biggest strengths: rare combination of ISO 13485, ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 certifications, in-house regulatory consultants for HIPAA, FDA and MDR, two decades of healthcare IT delivery.

2. IT Craft

IT Craft has built custom software since 2001 and brings more than 20 years of healthcare experience. Its 330+ specialists build EHR/EMR systems, telemedicine and remote patient monitoring platforms, patient portals, medical billing and RCM software, LIMS and software for medical devices.

Teams develop to HIPAA, GDPR, HL7 FHIR, FDA, MDR and IEC 62304 requirements and integrate with Epic, DICOM and other EHR systems. Recent work includes a HIPAA-compliant SaaS platform for legal-medical workflows and HIPAA-compliant infrastructure for a claims-auditing startup.

Best for: windows / desktop application development, healthcare startups, legacy modernization with AI integration , clinics, hospitals and medical device makers that need one partner from MVP through enterprise scale, with medical software audits, security fixes and 24/7 support included.

Biggest strengths: broad compliance coverage across HIPAA, GDPR, HL7 FHIR, FDA and IEC 62304, proven EHR and Epic integration experience, AI-powered solutions for diagnostics and clinical workflow automation.

3. Taction Software

Taction Software has worked exclusively in healthcare since 2013 and reports more than 250 completed healthcare and EHR integrations. It works with Epic, Oracle Health, HL7 v2, FHIR R4, X12 EDI and Mirth Connect, and holds ISO 27001 and ISO 9001 certifications plus a CMMI Level 3 appraisal. Biggest strengths: healthcare-only focus since 2013, hands-on experience with Epic, Oracle Health, HL7, FHIR and X12, BAA signed before the first line of code.

4. HTD Health

HTD Health is a strategy and technology consultancy dedicated to healthcare, with offices in New York, Poland and Argentina. It combines strategy advisory, human-centered product design and engineering, and builds FHIR applications for all major EMR systems. Its credentials include ISO 27001, ISO 27018 and ISO 13485; past clients include Boston Children’s Hospital and 1upHealth.

Best for: digital health companies that want product strategy, UX and compliant engineering from one team.

Biggest strengths: strategy, UX design and engineering under one roof, strong FHIR and EMR integration expertise, ISO 27001, ISO 27018 and ISO 13485 credentials.

5. Keyhole Software

Keyhole Software has delivered custom development since 2008 through 100% US-based employee consultants who average more than 17 years of experience. It has served 250+ clients, including healthcare providers such as Northwell Health, and specializes in modernizing mission-critical Java, .NET and cloud systems.

Best for: organizations that require senior, onshore engineers to modernize legacy healthcare platforms.

Biggest strengths: 100% US-based senior consultants, deep legacy modernization experience in Java and .NET, high client retention with most work coming from repeat clients.

Conclusion

Choosing a healthcare software partner requires more than comparing development costs and technical skills. The right firm should understand which regulations apply, sign the necessary agreements, document its security practices and build access controls, encryption, audit logging and incident response into the product from the beginning.

Before signing a contract, healthcare organizations should verify certifications, review relevant project experience and confirm who will be responsible for compliance after launch. A capable development partner can support that work, but responsibility for protecting patient data remains with everyone involved in building and operating the software.

item.title: Nearly 480,000 Phishing Emails Traced to Computer Hidden Behind Hotel Fridge
item.description:
A computer hidden behind a hotel room refrigerator in Kobe was allegedly used to send around 480,000 phishing emails, according to Japanese investigators. A Chinese couple living in the city have been arrested in connection with the email campaign and separate purchases made using another person’s credit card details.

The suspects are Ye Jiafeng, 39, and his wife, Shen Qi, 39. Ye faces allegations of fraudulent obstruction of business and trespass over the hotel incident, while both were arrested on suspicion of computer fraud over the alleged credit card purchases. Police have not disclosed their response to the allegations.

Computer Hidden Behind Hotel Refrigerator

On 15 May, 2025, Ye allegedly entered a Kobe hotel with another person, pretending to be a guest. The pair hid a small computer behind the room’s refrigerator and left it connected to the hotel’s Wi-Fi.

The scheme came to light after a recipient of the phishing emails contacted the hotel because its IP address appeared in information linked to the messages. Hotel staff found the computer and reported the matter to police.

The seized computer contained around 2.4 million email addresses and records of approximately 480,000 emails sent. The messages posed as communications from credit card companies and directed recipients to fake websites that captured their card details and other personal information. Investigators believe another person controlled the computer remotely and sent the emails through the hotel’s internet connection.

The case is not the first reported abuse of hotel internet infrastructure. In July 2026, Hackread.com reported on attackers who compromised hotel Wi-Fi gateways to redirect users to fake Microsoft 365 login pages. In the Kobe case, however, the alleged method involved hiding a computer on the network rather than hacking into the hotel’s Wi-Fi equipment.

Police Probe Other Suspected Fraud

The phishing investigation is not the only case involving the couple. In January 2026, Ye and Shen allegedly used a smartphone containing another person’s credit card details to buy three items, including down jackets, worth about 470,000 yen (approximately HK$24,000) at a commercial facility in Kobe.

Japanese media reported that police also recovered 74 smartphones from their home. Further investigation revealed that the couple had been using other people’s card details to make purchases since around 2024, with the total value amounting to 10 million yen. Police are examining the confiscated phones to identify the source of the card information and whether others were affected.

The couple was indicted in September 2026 in a separate case involving phishing emails sent through another Kobe hotel’s Wi-Fi and purchases made with other people’s card details. Police are investigating whether other people directed the activity or helped run the operation.

The couple’s response to the latest allegations has not been made public. The case does not necessarily indicate a weakness in the hotel’s Wi-Fi security. Investigators believe the computer was physically hidden in a guest room and left connected to the hotel’s network for remote use.

Dr. Aleksandr Yampolskiy, Co-Founder and CEO at SecurityScorecard, said the case highlights how criminals can exploit a business’s internet connection without necessarily breaching its systems. He shared the following comments with Hackread.com:

“What makes this case unusual is that the suspects allegedly brought their own equipment into a legitimate business rather than compromising its systems. By hiding a computer in a hotel room and controlling it remotely, the operators could use the hotel’s internet connection to send phishing emails without being physically present.

“Using a legitimate network does not automatically make phishing emails harder for security tools to detect, but it can make the people behind the operation more difficult to trace. Investigators following the network activity may initially be led to the hotel rather than the individuals controlling the device.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Samsung Black Friday 2026: Galaxy Offers to Look Out For (2026)
item.description:
Black Friday 2026 is coming! Explore Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra, S24, foldable phones, tablets and watches, plus refurbished deals, savings and buying tips.

Black Friday falls on November 27 this year, and Samsung’s Galaxy range tends to draw plenty of attention once the discounts begin. A little planning can make the season less hectic, starting with knowing which devices are worth watching and what to check before buying.

Why the Galaxy S25 Ultra Leads the List

The Galaxy S25 Ultra sits at the top of many Samsung wish lists, and the specs explain why. It pairs a Snapdragon 8 Elite chip with a 6.9-inch display and a 200-megapixel main camera, while the S Pen stays tucked inside the body. Storage options reach 1TB.

A refurbished Galaxy S25 Ultra on Back Market offers a way to get that hardware for less. Back Market is a global marketplace dedicated to extending the lifespan of electronic devices through refurbishment and circularity.

Trust matters when buying a refurbished flagship, so the checks are worth knowing. Back Market says each device goes through an inspection of up to 100 points before it is listed, and its devices carry a minimum of 80% battery health. The newest model is not the only one worth a look, though.

Older Galaxy Models Still Earn Their Place

Scroll through the Samsung Black Friday selection, and the Galaxy S24 appears on Back Market next to older models such as the Z Fold6 and Z Flip5.

The Galaxy S24 launched with a promise of seven years of Android and security updates, which gives it a long runway as a refurbished phone. Software support matters as much as hardware, since it affects both security and everyday use.

Listings also show whether a phone is unlocked or tied to a single carrier. Reading that label before checkout can prevent surprises, because unlocked phones work with any U.S. carrier.

Tablets and Watches Join the Sale

Samsung’s ecosystem reaches beyond phones, and Back Market lists refurbished Galaxy Tab models alongside Galaxy Watch options. A tablet suits streaming and note-taking, while a watch brings fitness tracking to the wrist.

This Black Friday, Back Market offers refurbished Samsung Galaxy phones and tablets with significant savings and warranty included. That warranty lasts one year, and returns are free for 30 days, which leaves time to test a device before committing.

Pairing a phone with a tablet or watch from the same brand tends to keep setup simple, since accounts and apps carry across Galaxy devices. Whichever device ends up in the cart, its condition grade shapes the price.

Why Refurbished Samsung Devices Make Sense

Condition grades add clarity. Back Market uses four grades, from Fair to Premium, and all of them are described as fully functional, with the difference limited to cosmetic wear. That lets you pick a price level without giving up core performance.

There is an environmental angle too. Back Market estimates, using a 2022 study by the French agency ADEME, that a refurbished phone avoids about 92% of the manufacturing emissions of a new one.

Where to buy an iPhone on Black Friday? The same logic applies, since Back Market lists refurbished iPhones alongside its Galaxy range. With the date set for November 27, a short wish list and a quick check of grade and warranty will keep the season simple.

item.title: Scammers Abuse Frame.io Notifications to Steal Microsoft 365 Credentials
item.description:
Ocean Security found a phishing campaign, dubbed Phantom Preview, that abused legitimate Frame.io notifications and hidden PDF links to deliver fake Microsoft 365 login pages.

Cybersecurity researchers at Ocean Security identified a targeted adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing campaign on August 27, 2026, that abused Adobe Frame.io‘s legitimate share notifications to evade conventional email security checks.

Dubbed Phantom Preview, the campaign used a PDF to conceal a link to a fake Microsoft 365 login page that sent 22 emails to a single enterprise tenant within two hours. The messages came from the legitimate address [email protected] using the subject line “Jason Pitts shared ‘BTF Project’ with you,” making them appear to be routine file-sharing notifications.

The initial link led to Frame.io‘s genuine platform, where the shared PDF appeared as a non-clickable preview. The research, shared with Hackread.com, explains that this prevented the scanners investigating the share page from readily identifying the malicious destination hidden inside the original document.

An employee reported the first suspicious email just three minutes after it arrived, but conventional security checks had not flagged the threat.

AI Agent Traced the Hidden Link

Ocean Security used its AI investigation agent, Ray, to retrieve the original PDF through Frame.io‘s GraphQL GetAssetForDownload path. The agent examined the document’s /URI annotations, which specify link destinations, and uncovered a URL concealed behind the preview.

Ray also searched the tenant’s email history using the campaign’s subject line, identifying 21 other matching messages.

The link hidden inside the PDF redirected targets through a Cloudflare Pages subdomain using a 301 redirect. It then sent victims to a newly registered domain, msauth.biz. It was registered via eNom on August 6, 2026, and hosted on DigitalOcean.

When researchers checked it, VirusTotal showed zero detections across 91 security engines. This means the domain had not been flagged by any of those engines at the time.

The site used a Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA to make it harder for security tools to check the page automatically. After a visitor passed the test, JavaScript created a URL containing a unique token, such as ?s=gQpS40I, that led to a fake Microsoft 365 login page.

According to Ocean Security, the token was designed to prevent the link from being easily shared or reused. This helped the attackers keep the phishing page tied to its intended victim.

Defending Against Trusted Share Notifications

Ocean Security has confirmed that Frame.io itself was not compromised. The attackers used its legitimate sharing system to send phishing emails that looked like normal file notifications.

Researchers recommend checking the files behind these notifications, not just the email sender or the link. In particular, security teams should check PDFs for hidden links to unfamiliar websites, including newly registered domains and suspicious Cloudflare Pages addresses.

item.title: BAE Systems Cyber Incident Disrupts US Bankruptcy Notices
item.description:
A cyber incident affecting BAE Systems halted US bankruptcy notices, forcing federal courts to change service procedures and adjust some deadlines.

A cybersecurity incident affecting systems operated by BAE Systems Inc. has halted the production and distribution of official notices for US bankruptcy cases. The nationwide outage began on October 9, 2026, disrupting paper and electronic notices sent to creditors, debtors and other parties.

The Administrative Office of the US Courts confirmed the incident on October 15. BAE Systems Inc., the US subsidiary of British defence company BAE Systems plc, operates the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC) systems and websites on behalf of the federal judiciary.

Bankruptcy Notice Websites Offline

The outage has taken several websites offline, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov and notices.uscourts.gov. The National Creditor Registration Service is also unavailable.

“As a result of the incident, all access to the BNC systems and websites that BAE operates on behalf of the judiciary and the related bankruptcy noticing process are unavailable at this time,” the US Courts said.

Federal bankruptcy courts continue to accept filings and process cases, but the outage has stopped paper notices and electronic notices normally distributed through the BNC. Electronic notifications sent directly to registered CM/ECF users remain available in at least some districts, according to an update from the Eastern District of Tennessee.

The outage is also preventing some CM/ECF users from generating or printing creditor lists, sometimes called mailing matrices. Parties who depend on BNC delivery may therefore receive delayed information about hearings, court orders and case filings.

Courts Change Notice Procedures and Deadlines

Because bankruptcy courts administer their own local procedures, responses have varied by district.

Courts have introduced different measures to manage the disruption. In the Southern District of Florida, an order issued on October 16 requires trustees, debtors and their lawyers to handle certain notices normally sent through the BNC. The Eastern District of Louisiana has also assigned responsibility for mailing specified notices to debtors and trustees in certain cases filed since October 7.

Other courts have addressed proceedings affected by missing notices. The Southern District of Indiana and the Middle District of Pennsylvania directed that creditor meetings be adjourned, not concluded, when the outage prevents proper notice from being delivered.

The Southern District of Texas is allowing parties to request deadline extensions, with relief decided individually. Most courts have not introduced automatic deadline extensions, although the Middle District of Florida extended certain service deadlines, while the Eastern District of Texas granted a 30-day extension of the automatic stay in qualifying cases.

BAE Systems Investigating Incident

BAE Systems Inc. said the security incident was isolated to the BNC system and that no other company systems were affected. The company is working with the Administrative Office of the US Courts to restore the affected services.

Neither organisation has disclosed the cause, identified an attacker or said whether bankruptcy data was accessed or stolen. No restoration date had been announced at the time of writing.

Experts Warn of Risks From Reliance on Third-Party Systems

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, shared his comments with Hackread.com, saying the incident highlights how closely business and government processes are connected.

“A lot of people still think about computer security in terms of a DMZ. There’s an internal network to protect and an outside world to protect it from. But look at any modern large organization. They have multiple SaaS platforms, third-party integrations, and customer data flowing in and out of systems they don’t own or control. That perimeter is a lot messier than people want to believe.”

“I still don’t think the industry has caught up with the risks we introduced through cloud computing and SaaS. Now we’re adding AI to the mix, giving attackers new ways to target those services and exploit the connections between them. We weren’t caught up before. We’re certainly not ready now,” Strand added.

Jacob Krell, Senior Director of Secure AI Solutions and Cybersecurity at Suzu Labs, also shared his comments with Hackread.com, describing bankruptcy notices as “the machinery of due process” and pointing to the judiciary’s reliance on one contractor.

“Judges are already compensating, extending deadlines and continuing hearings district by district. That is the detail that should worry anyone procuring for the courts. The outage never touched a courtroom, yet it rewrote the calendar of every bankruptcy case in the country, because a vendor bought like routine IT has become load-bearing infrastructure for the justice system.”

“Restoring service is the urgent job. The standing question is why the noticing architecture has no alternate path, and I would want the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts to write continuity requirements into the next BAE contract as strict as the ones the courts impose on themselves,” explained Krell.

item.title: Live Video Moderation Challenges Traditional Content Safety Systems
item.description:
Learn how live video moderation handles frame sampling, end-to-end encryption, behavioural signals, privacy and content retention in video chat.

Most content-moderation systems were developed around material that can be inspected before publication or reviewed after it has been uploaded. Live video gives platforms far less time to act.

Images and recorded videos can be hashed, compared with databases of known illegal material and sent for human review. Microsoft, for example, says it uses PhotoDNA and MD5 to identify known harmful image and video content on its consumer services.

Live services can also inspect frames or short video segments while a session is active. The technical problem is timing. Detection must happen quickly enough to interrupt the broadcast, warn participants or limit further exposure, even though some frames may already have reached viewers.

That time pressure affects how detection models, human review, encryption and retention can be used. Live moderation is not impossible, but it requires different technical and policy choices from moderation built around uploaded files.

Live Video Leaves Little Time to Act

Interactive video is sensitive to delay. Capture, encoding, transmission and playback already consume part of the available processing time, leaving moderation systems to work without making the conversation noticeably slower.

Human reviewers cannot assess every live session before content reaches another participant. Automated systems therefore perform the first assessment, with people handling reports, disputed decisions and cases referred for further examination.

Platforms may also respond without immediately ending a session. A detection result could increase monitoring, blur video, display a warning, restrict an account or send the activity for review. The available response depends on the severity of the material and the confidence of the detection model.

AWS has published an example live-content moderation workflow that extracts frames from a live channel, analyses them, stores selected frames and stops the broadcast when specified content is detected. It shows that live analysis is technically possible, although the design still has to account for processing cost, delay and detection errors.

Frame Sampling Creates a Detection Gap

Many services reduce processing demands by sampling frames or short clips instead of analysing every frame. The chosen rate depends on available computing power, session volume, device capabilities and the type of harm being detected.

Sampling introduces an unavoidable trade-off. Inspecting fewer frames reduces processing costs but creates a longer period in which prohibited material could appear and disappear between checks. Increasing the rate gives the system more opportunities to detect that material but requires more computing resources.

Fixed sampling is not the only option. A platform can begin with a lower rate and increase it when other signals indicate greater risk. A new account receiving several reports, repeated rapid disconnections or suspicious device activity could trigger more frequent analysis.

Anyone assessing a platform’s moderation claims should therefore ask how often content is examined, which events increase that frequency and what happens after a model returns an uncertain result.

Where the Detection Model Runs

The location of the moderation model affects privacy, performance and resistance to tampering. The three main approaches are server-side, on-device and hybrid processing.

Server-side processing gives a platform greater control over model updates and computing resources. It also requires access to video in a form the server can inspect, creating privacy, security and legal concerns.

On-device processing keeps raw content closer to the user, but the model runs on hardware outside the platform’s control. Attackers may modify the application, disable checks or study the model to identify inputs it handles poorly.

Hybrid systems use local screening before sending selected material for additional analysis. This can limit how much video reaches the server, but it does not remove the weaknesses associated with either location.

Why End-to-End Encryption Rules Out Server-Side Content Inspection

A platform cannot claim that only participants can access a session while also decrypting that session on its servers for content analysis. Server-side inspection of plaintext conflicts with the defining privacy guarantee of end-to-end encryption.

Client-side scanning has been proposed as a way to inspect content before encryption or after decryption on the recipient’s device. The approach has faced sustained opposition from security and privacy researchers.

In Bugs in Our Pockets, fourteen cryptographers and security researchers examined how client-side scanning could be evaded, repurposed or abused. They argued that placing a scanning capability on personal devices creates risks extending past the original categories of content it was designed to identify.

The paper appeared as a preprint in 2021 before being published in the Journal of Cybersecurity in 2024. Its objections apply to stored material and communications inspected on user devices, including video analysed before transmission.

End-to-end encryption does not prevent every form of moderation. User reporting, account restrictions and metadata analysis remain available without giving the platform routine access to session content.

A separate study of moderation in encrypted systems found that reporting and metadata-based methods were more likely to preserve the privacy and security properties expected from encrypted services.

Behavioural Signals Do Not Require Access to Video

Live services can examine how accounts behave without analysing what appears on camera. Useful signals may include session duration, repeated reconnections, report history, account age, device information and how frequently participants end conversations within the first few seconds.

Services operating video chat for large user bases can use these signals to support frame or clip analysis. A single image may be unclear, while repeated account behaviour can show a pattern that deserves review.

Behavioural analysis is not a complete substitute for inspecting content. It can identify repeated activity, coordinated abuse or attempts to return after suspension, but it may miss a first-time offender or a harmful event with no prior warning.

This form of monitoring also carries privacy obligations. Account histories, device reputation and behavioural profiles may involve additional data collection and automated decision-making. Platforms should document what they collect, why they collect it and how long the information is retained.

Retention Creates Another Privacy Decision

Reports often arrive after a session has ended. A platform that retains nothing may have little evidence available to investigate, while one that records every session creates an archive of private video that could be exposed, misused or demanded through legal processes.

A safer approach is to retain the minimum material needed for a documented purpose, restrict access, encrypt it and delete it under an enforced schedule. The retention period should reflect reporting delays, safeguarding requirements and legal obligations.

Some services may retain sampled frames or short encrypted buffers associated with a specific session. Access can then be limited to authorised reviews initiated by a user report or a high-confidence automated alert.

Users should be told whether sessions are recorded, whether sampled images are retained, who can access them and when deletion occurs. Those choices belong in the product’s privacy and security design, not only in an internal operations document.

Questions Platforms Should Answer

Live video moderation is not uploaded-image moderation performed faster. It combines time-sensitive detection, incomplete sampling, privacy limits and decisions about where analysis takes place.

Anyone evaluating a live-video service should ask where inference runs, how often frames or clips are examined, which events increase monitoring and how long any retained content remains available.

Those answers reveal more about a platform’s moderation and privacy choices than a general commitment to user safety.

An avid writer with a keen interest in technological developments, he focuses on making complex topics accessible to readers while examining their impact on businesses and everyday users.

item.title: Multi-Cloud Blind Spots Are Leaving Security Teams Exposed
item.description:
Most enterprises didn’t choose multi-cloud as a deliberate strategy. They ended up there: an acquisition brought in a company already running on a different provider, one team picked Amazon Web Services (AWS) because that’s what they knew, another spun up projects in Microsoft Azure because it bundled with existing licensing, and a third quietly built things in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) because a developer liked the tooling.

Nobody sat down and designed this. And nobody ended up owning the gaps between the pieces. That’s the actual risk. Not any single cloud provider, but the seams where they meet.

Why the seams are the problem

Each cloud provider has its own identity and access management (IAM) model, its own default settings, its own way of structuring permissions and resources. A security policy that’s airtight in AWS doesn’t automatically carry the same meaning in Azure, even when the two look conceptually similar on paper.

Teams that assume parity across providers, treating “we locked this down in one cloud” as equivalent to “we locked this down everywhere,” are often wrong without realizing it, because the underlying models simply don’t map one to one.

This isn’t a hypothetical concern. It’s the quiet reality behind a lot of the incidents that get reported after the fact: not a single dramatic failure, but a gap between two systems that nobody was responsible for checking.

Shadow resources nobody’s tracking

When different teams provision infrastructure in different clouds independently, asset inventories fall out of sync fast. A test environment spun up in one provider for a project that ended months ago doesn’t disappear on its own.

It sits there, outside whatever dashboard the security team actually watches, until it becomes exactly the kind of overlooked resource that shows up again and again in misconfiguration-driven incidents. The problem isn’t that any one team did something careless. It’s that nobody had a complete picture of what existed across all the environments at once.

Inconsistent logging means inconsistent detection

Visibility is the other casualty of multi-cloud sprawl. Different providers log different events by default, in different formats, retained for different lengths of time. A security team that built its detection pipeline around one provider’s logging conventions can have real blind spots into the others, and the gap often isn’t obvious until an investigation reveals that the data needed simply isn’t there, or was deleted before anyone thought to look for it.

Why this calls for cross-provider thinking, not provider-specific expertise

This is exactly the problem that a credential built around reasoning about cloud security across providers, rather than mastering one platform’s console, is meant to address. The Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP) credential from the International Information System Security Certification Consortium (ISC2) covers six domains, including cloud platform and infrastructure security and cloud data security, built specifically around the idea that “cloud security” isn’t one skill tied to one vendor; it’s a way of thinking that has to hold up regardless of which provider is in play.

“The seams between clouds are where most of this risk actually lives, not inside any single provider,” says Rob Witcher, co-founder of Destination Certification. “A team can be excellent at securing AWS and excellent at securing Azure separately and still have a massive gap in between, because nobody’s job is to look at the two together.” That’s the gap CCSP training is actually built to close: not provider-specific know-how, but the judgment to see risk across all of them at once.

What actually closes the gap

None of this requires abandoning multi-cloud or consolidating onto a single provider, which usually isn’t realistic anyway once an organization has grown into it. It requires a few deliberate changes: a consolidated view that shows assets and configurations across every provider in one place, rather than three separate dashboards nobody cross-references.

Logging standards applied consistently on purpose, rather than inherited by accident from whatever each provider happens to default to. And a named owner for cross-cloud risk specifically, someone whose job is to look at the seams, rather than three separate teams each assuming the gap between their clouds is someone else’s problem.

item.title: Industrial Defender Unifies Endpoint Intelligence and Network Monitoring for CIP-015, Adds Risk Signal
item.description:
Orlando, Florida, United States, October 20th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Industrial Defender Unifies Endpoint Intelligence and Network Monitoring for CIP-015, Adds Risk Signal to Turn Findings into Prioritized Patch Plans

New internal network security monitoring correlates every anomaly with deep asset intelligence; Risk Signal converts findings into verified remediation

Industrial Defender, an OT cybersecurity leader serving the global critical infrastructure industry, today released its latest version, adding internal network security monitoring (INSM) and Risk Signal.

The release builds on Industrial Defender’s decades of leadership serving NERC-CIP regulated utilities, pairing its deep endpoint visibility with network traffic monitoring, providing OT/ICS operators a single path from detection to prioritized remediation.

“Network monitoring tells you something changed. Our customers need to know what that change means and what to do next,” said George Kalavantis, Chief Executive Officer, Industrial Defender.

The FERC-approved NERC CIP-015-1 standard requires entities with high and medium impact BES Cyber Systems to monitor internal network traffic, detect and evaluate anomalies, and retain and protect the resulting data.

Built into the existing platform, the INSM solution learns each device’s baseline communications and flags deviations such as new connections, unexpected protocols, anomalous traffic volume and unknown devices communicating.

“Our platform now associates network traffic with deep endpoint intelligence to provide a more comprehensive cybersecurity,” Kalavantis said.

Each anomaly is correlated with the asset data Industrial Defender maintains, including configuration changes, vulnerabilities and risk score, so operators understand immediately what a network change means to operations.

Every review decision is captured with reviewer, timestamp and rationale, creating audit-ready evidence mapped to CIP-015 requirements.

Beyond CIP-015, INSM serves industrial control system environments across sectors like oil & gas, petrochemical processing and manufacturing, connecting rich asset data with network visibility to strengthen cybersecurity posture.

Risk Signal: Patch what matters first

Detection and visibility are only half the job. Risk Signal closes the loop by turning asset, vulnerability and network findings into action.

Building on each customer’s existing risk model, it identifies the patches and upgrades that deliver the greatest risk reduction for the least operational effort, then packages them into prioritized playbooks that publish directly into existing work-management systems.

After remediation, Risk Signal verifies each patch was applied and updates the asset’s risk score.

“The latest version of our trusted platform connects network activity with the asset intelligence we’ve engineered for two decades, and Risk Signal turns that insight into a defensible plan. It’s the shortest path from visibility to reduced risk for critical infrastructure” Kalavantis said.

Industrial Defender will demonstrate these capabilities at GridSecCon 2026 in Orlando.

About Industrial Defender

Industrial Defender provides OT and ICS cybersecurity and compliance solutions for critical infrastructure operators, including electric utilities, oil & gas, chemical, water, and manufacturing organizations. The platform delivers continuous OT asset visibility, vulnerability management, and audit-ready compliance reporting across frameworks including NERC CIP, NIS2, IEC 62443, and NIST CSF.

item.title: China-Based BRONZE SANDCASTLE Hackers Abuse Sandboxie to Load Backdoors
item.description:
Sophos found BRONZE SANDCASTLE abusing legitimate Windows apps to load encrypted backdoors, collect system information and steal Active Directory data.

A China-based hacking group is using legitimate Windows applications to load encrypted backdoors onto organisations’ systems in Asia and Africa, according to research from Sophos CTU and Sophos Labs.

Researchers tracked BRONZE SANDCASTLE activity between August 2025 and August 2026, identifying victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan and Namibia, with South Korea also considered a likely victim location.

Sandboxie, software designed to run applications in an isolated environment, appeared repeatedly in the attacks. The operators placed a legitimate Sandboxie executable alongside a malicious DLL, which it loaded when launched. The research does not report a compromise of Sandboxie’s website or official downloads.

Legitimate Software Loads Encrypted Payloads

According to Sophos’ research shared with Hackread.com, the group used DLL sideloading to execute its malware. Other abused applications included Java, Krita, NVDA, LINE, and Sysinternals utilities.

When the legitimate program starts, the malicious DLL opens config.ini, decrypts the backdoor stored inside and runs it in memory. The attackers can update that file to change what the backdoor does without replacing the DLL. Since the payload stays encrypted on disk, file scans may miss code that becomes visible only when it runs.

Backdoors Collect System Details and Support Credential Theft

Sophos identified payload versions 1.1.5 and 1.1.7, describing a modified Meterpreter-based backdoor with custom loading behaviour. Once running, it collects host and process information and communicates with command servers. Version 1.1.7 also retrieved encrypted configuration files from GitHub repositories.

After gaining access, operators examined networks and user accounts. Researchers also observed them creating Windows Volume Shadow Copies and copying ntds.dit, the Active Directory database containing domain account information and password hashes.

Sophos Keeps Attribution Separate From Similar Campaigns

Although other groups including BRONZE PRESIDENT (aka HoneyMate and Mustang Panda)target similar locations, Sophos could not reliably connect their activity to BRONZE SANDCASTLE. Its repeated use of Sandboxie sideloading helped researchers distinguish the group’s operations.

Organisations checking for these attacks should examine what recognised applications load and execute, including unexpected libraries and encrypted files followed by activity in memory. Trusting an executable’s name or origin alone leaves the malicious components it launches unchecked.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: INC and The Gentlemen Ransomware Affiliates Expose 8,257 AI Messages
item.description:
SOCRadar has found seven exposed servers linked to INC and The Gentlemen ransomware affiliates, holding AI chats, stolen credentials and 46 encryptor builds.

Cybersecurity researchers at SOCRadar recently discovered seven exposed servers linked to INC Ransomware and The Gentlemen ransomware affiliates, finding AI session logs, stolen credentials and ransomware tools among the exposed data.

According to the company’s report, published on October 20, the SOCRadar Threat Research Unit (STRU) recovered 8,257 AI messages across 133 OpenCode sessions, along with 46 custom INC encryptor builds prepared for six victims.

The records also indicated more than $23,920 in AI API spending, and the use of commercial models by the operators, including Claude Opus 4.6 and Kimi K3.

AI-Assisted Intrusions Remained Under Human Control

The operators used OpenCode, an AI coding interface, alongside persistent knowledge bases to plan reconnaissance, generate commands, analyze stolen credentials and draft reports.

The session logs show that human approval was required before each step. One instruction told the AI to “coordinate every action with me,” indicating that the operators retained control over the attack process.

When commercial models refused malicious requests, the operators rephrased their prompts as “Authorized Red Team Assessment Request” templates. This suggests they tried to get around the models’ refusals through prompt changes rather than switching to different models.

Exploited Vulnerabilities and Custom Tools

According to operator records analyzed by STRU in its report, the affiliates targeted internet-facing systems and remote-access infrastructure, including:

  1. CVE-2026-41940 (cPanel): Operators claimed more than 49 breaches of hosting providers.
  2. CVE-2024-57727 (SimpleHelp): Scans of 4,922 servers reportedly yielded 427 administrator passwords, with 242 unique IP addresses listed as impacted.
  3. CVE-2026-35616 (FortiClient EMS): Records claimed 2,236 targets, 108 newly created administrator accounts and 4,140 managed endpoints.

These figures come from the attackers’ records and have not been independently verified. The exposed servers also contained WormGPT-labelled MCP server, Phantom, a custom framework for coordinating attack activities, alongside command-and-control tools and software designed to disable security products.

Ransomware Builds and Victim Records

The investigation identified 62 named organizations in the operators’ records, including 36 in the United States. Industrial and manufacturing organizations accounted for 16.1% of the listed targets, followed by healthcare and pharmaceutical organizations at 14.5%.

Although 46 INC encryptor builds were prepared for six victims ahead of a planned October 1, 2026, deployment, the report does not confirm that all six attacks took place. A September 30 screenshot from a SimpleHelp console showed an encryptor running on a victim workstation, providing evidence of encryption activity in at least one case.

The records also described an extortion strategy built around stolen financial and business data, with threats to contact victims’ customers, partners and regulators. The findings offer a rare look at how ransomware operators used AI during active intrusions while retaining human oversight.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.
